passage_answers.before: The reader first meets the right zero vector, the normalized left zero vector and how v removes decaying modes. The local system then defines x, y, a and lambda and derives x(infinity). The figure arrives only after those terms and relationships have meaning.
passage_answers.reader_question: If I impose a vertical displacement, which point is kept as the memory after the state relaxes?
passage_answers.answer_without_expert_filling: At a/lambda=1/2, the drawing specifies a jump from (0,0) to (0,2) and a straight recovery toward (1,0). Its separate perpendicular foot shows why returning to (0,0) would be the wrong prediction. The lower formula extracts the change of one.
passage_answers.after: The interpretation states what changed in the same example. The next section then applies the already-defined v^T projection to spike noise. The example supplies the purpose of that multiplication before the algebra begins.
passage_answers.assumptions: Dimensionless exact linear teaching system, lambda positive and a/lambda=1/2; it is explicitly distinguished from a paper-network simulation. The asymptotic endpoint language is preserved.

paragraph_purpose.intro: Focuses the reader on flow versus perpendicular projection.
paragraph_purpose.caption: Fixes the numerical example and identifies its source status; the repaired sentence clearly separates imposed jump from subsequent relaxation.
paragraph_purpose.alt: Supplies the geometric distinctions and functional role for a reader without the image.
paragraph_purpose.interpretation: States the retained shift and returns to the projection argument.

passage_answers.unresolved_reader_gap: None in this local insertion. The reader need not already know oblique projection theory; the system, endpoint and contrast provide it concretely.

new_passages.intro: The exact trajectory in this example shows why the lasting displacement follows the flow rather than a perpendicular projection.
new_passages.caption: Original guide construction of the tilted decay example, with dimensionless coordinates and $a/\lambda=1/2$. After an imposed jump from $(0,0)$ to $(0,2)$, the state relaxes toward $(1,0)$; successive time marks crowd toward that endpoint. This illustrates the left and right zero vector construction in Burak and Fiete (2012), Supporting Text, Section II, pp. 3–4, Eqs. S10–S16; it is not a paper network simulation.
new_passages.alt: A line of fixed points lies at y equals zero. An imposed vertical jump from zero zero to zero two is followed by a straight tilted flow toward one zero. Equal time marks crowd toward the endpoint. Perpendicular projection would return to zero zero and miss the lasting shift of one. The tangent is one zero; the left vector measures delta x plus one half delta y.
new_passages.interpretation: As y decays, x changes by one; the left vector extracts that lasting shift.

passage_answers.before: The section first defines the cue time, original value, cue state, storage displacement and readout error. It writes the covariance term and explains conditional unbiasedness, future-noise independence and translation invariance before giving the summed variance.
passage_answers.reader_question: Which value do later spikes estimate, and why is the uncertainty from storage still present?
passage_answers.answer_without_expert_filling: The separate cue point and estimate diamond refer to the same cue state, while the path keeps moving beyond it. The storage and readout brackets are the two already-defined differences. The estimate is not the terminal state, and the caption repeats why the variance terms may be added.
passage_answers.after: The interpretation reminds the reader what cannot be recovered from future spikes. The next paragraph turns to the Gaussian observation model for estimating that cue state, so the figure finishes defining the estimation problem before the solution begins.
passage_answers.assumptions: Constant diffusion on an unbounded coordinate without drift; locally unbiased readout at every cue state, independent future noise and translation-invariant variance. They are explained in adjacent prose and listed in the unchanged artwork.

paragraph_purpose.intro: Identifies the two errors on the time line.
paragraph_purpose.caption: Explains which state the estimate concerns and retains the zero-covariance condition.
paragraph_purpose.alt: Preserves time order, bracket definitions, separate estimate and assumptions.
paragraph_purpose.interpretation: Connects the visual separation back to the inference limit.

passage_answers.unresolved_reader_gap: None in this local insertion. The reader sees the conditional covariance reasoning before the figure and does not have to supply an independence argument.

new_passages.intro: A timeline separates the displacement accumulated before the cue from the error in estimating the cue state afterward.
new_passages.caption: Original guide construction of storage and cue state readout, based on Burak and Fiete (2012), Supporting Text, p. 12, Eq. S57. The illustrated path is one possible construction, and the orange estimate concerns the state at the cue rather than the state at the end of observation. With the conditions shown, storage and readout variances add because their cross covariance is zero.
new_passages.alt: The stored value starts at Theta at encoding time zero and wanders until the recall cue at T. Its cue value is x. Later spikes, collected through T plus L, give an estimate x hat of that cue state. Storage error is x minus Theta; readout error is x hat minus x. The estimate is drawn separately from the path endpoint. Under the listed independence, unbiasedness and translation assumptions, total variance is two D T plus readout variance.
new_passages.interpretation: Later spikes can improve the estimate of $x=\theta(T)$; they do not reveal the particular storage displacements that separated $x$ from $\Theta$.

passage_answers.before: The simple-average and ideal-observer formulas have already been derived, including coth and the duration scale. The immediately preceding paragraph restates the two rescaled formulas, their minimum, short-duration divergence, limiting value and exclusion of 2DT.
passage_answers.reader_question: Why can collecting more observations worsen equal-weight readout while ideal readout still improves?
passage_answers.answer_without_expert_filling: The dashed equal-weight curve reaches its marked minimum and rises, while the solid ideal curve falls toward one. The interpretation ties that rise to late observations of a state that has moved. The axes and caption identify these as readout-only variances.
passage_answers.after: The next paragraph separately examines the printed total-error bound. Because the caption explicitly excludes storage variance, the reader has a reason to distinguish the plotted readout scale from the upcoming total-error expression.
passage_answers.assumptions: The preceding local Gaussian, homogeneous, no-informative-prior readout model underlies the analytic formulas. The graph begins at positive z and directly labels the limiting divergence rather than assigning a value at zero.

paragraph_purpose.intro: States what the comparison makes visible after the formula recap.
paragraph_purpose.caption: Keeps the analytic source status, optimum, ideal limit and variance scope attached to the plot.
paragraph_purpose.alt: States the normalized axes and distinct curve behavior without the image.
paragraph_purpose.interpretation: Connects the mathematical contrast to the observation-weighting explanation.

passage_answers.unresolved_reader_gap: None in this local insertion. Both formulas, normalization scales, the meaning of equal weighting and the meaning of ideal cue-state readout are already taught.

new_passages.intro: The normalized curves make the eventual cost of equal weighting visible.
new_passages.caption: Original guide construction from the analytic readout formulas in Burak and Fiete (2012), Fig. 3 and Supporting Text, Eqs. S75 and S79–S81, rather than digitized data. Ideal readout approaches a normalized variance of one; simple averaging reaches $2/\sqrt3$ at $z=\sqrt3$ and then worsens. These curves contain no storage variance $2DT$.
new_passages.alt: Readout variance divided by square root of two D over J is plotted against z equals L times square root of two D J. Both curves diverge as z approaches zero. Ideal readout coth z falls toward one. Simple averaging z over three plus one over z reaches its minimum at square root of three, two over square root of three, and then rises. The storage variance is absent.
new_passages.interpretation: More observation keeps helping the ideal reader, with diminishing benefit, while equal weighting eventually gives too much influence to a state that has moved.
